chapter_theme: The third twenty move from the body to the household and the road: rules of touch and of marital union timed by the wife's cycle and the calendar, the cleansing and auspicious ordering of the house, days without Vedic recitation, festival days and the welcome of guests, the measure of dress and speech, sights and places to avoid, omens at departure, and deference to elders on the road.

41.reading: The verse reports that those with subtle knowledge of the texts do not put the eye's discharge into the eye, do not rub one foot against the other, and do not let other limbs touch the head, which it calls holy.
41.nuance: Line 2 is damaged: தலையோடு றுப்புறுத்த is read as the head with the other limbs pressed to it, a rule that the head, called புண்ணியம், is not touched by lower parts; the first rule, கண்ணெச்சில் கண்ணூட்டார், may instead bar touching the eye with a hand soiled by spittle.

norm.note: a purity rule of the period on how the body's parts may touch, with the head treated as holy

42.reading: The verse gives as the settled view of the greatly wise that a man does not look at his wife on the three days she may not be touched, and that after she has bathed he does not leave her for the twelve days that follow.
42.nuance: தீண்டாநாள் names the menstrual days by the bar on touch; the verse does not say why the twelve days after the bath matter, but setting them right after the bath ties the rule of pollution to the timing of marital union. The closing phrase பேரறி வாளர் துணிவு recurs from verse 19.

norm.note: a menstrual pollution rule of the period: the wife is not touched or looked at for three days, and the husband stays with her for twelve days after her bath

43.reading: The verse lists the times on which, it reports, husband and wife do not come together: noon, midnight, the two twilights, the days of the two great gods, the uvā tithi days, the eighth day of the moon, and one's birthday.
43.nuance: இருதேவர் நாள் is not explained; it names the festival days of two gods without saying which. டுவாத்திதிநாள் is read as உவா joined to திதிநாள், the new- and full-moon days, and taken as one item; ஏனைப் பிறந்தநாள் is read as the birth-star day.

items.claim: noon is a time when the couple do not come together
midnight is such a time
the two twilights are such times
the days of the two great gods are such days
the new- and full-moon tithi days are such days
the eighth day of the lunar fortnight is such a day
one's birthday is such a day

norm.note: a rule of the period setting the hours and calendar days on which marital union is barred

44.reading: The verse reports household rules: one does not set the measuring vessel down on the seat-plank or turn the plank over, does not unfold new cloth in the doorway, does not lie on a cot at the threshold without thought, and does not let strangers stand at one's head.
44.nuance: இரியார் and பாடஅர் are doubtful forms; பாடஅர் is read as படார், 'do not lie down', and the last rule, அறியாதார் தந்தலைக்கண் நில்லா விடல், can also mean keeping unknown people from standing at the head of the house. These look like rules of omen rather than of pollution.

norm.note: household omen rules of the period about the seat, new cloth, the threshold and strangers

45.reading: The verse names five things that are not to be spread inside the pandal: a broom, sweepings, dried grass and leaves, a black pot, and a torn cot.
45.nuance: துகள்காடு is taken as one thing, a heap of dust and sweepings, to reach the verse's five; split into dust and refuse the list would run to six. The pandal is presumably the booth raised for a wedding or festival, though the verse does not say so.

items.claim: a broom is not spread inside the pandal
sweepings and refuse are not spread there
dried grass and dead leaves are not spread there
a black pot is not spread there
a torn cot is not spread there

norm.note: a rule of the period keeping unclean and inauspicious things out of the festive booth

46.reading: The verse says that those who want good to come to them clear away the refuse, wash the vessels, sprinkle cow-dung water all through the house, fill the water-pot and the karakam early in the morning, adorn them with flowers, and light fire in the hearth so that the house shines.
46.nuance: The reason given is the household's fortune, நல்லது உறல், not purity as such: cleaning and lighting the hearth are read as making the house auspicious.

norm.note: a rule of the period for the morning cleansing of the house with cow-dung water and the first lighting of the hearth

47.reading: The verse lists the days on which brahmins do not recite the shining texts: the eighth day, the new and full moon, the fourteenth, a time of affliction to the one who guards the land, a great earthquake, thunder in the sky, and a state of impurity.
47.nuance: பார்ப்பார் names a birth-group whose duty is set here; the verse does not rank them against others but makes Vedic recitation theirs. The king's distress stands in the same list as earthquake and thunder, as a disturbance of the world that halts recitation.

items.claim: the eighth lunar day is a day without recitation
the new and full moon are such days
the fourteenth lunar day is such a day
affliction to the land's guardian halts recitation
a great earthquake halts it
thunder in the sky halts it
impurity halts it

norm.note: a rule of the period on the days a birth-group, the பார்ப்பார், suspend Vedic recitation, impurity among them

48.reading: The verse says that on five kinds of day, a wedding, the festivals of the gods and of the ancestors, other festivals and a sacrifice, one does aram without slighting it, and serves food to guests as well.
48.nuance: Line 1 names four occasions; the five of ஐவகை are reached by taking தேவர் and பிதிர் each with விழா and விழா again as festivals in general. விருந்திற்கும் 'for guests too' makes feeding guests the added duty of the day, after aram.

items.claim: a wedding day is a day for doing aram
the festival of the gods is such a day
the festival of the ancestors is such a day
a festival is such a day
a sacrifice is such a day

norm.note: a rule of the period for the festival and rite days of the household calendar

49.reading: The verse says that dress, gait, slackness of speech and rebuke, these four, are to be done as befits one's standing, learning, manliness and family.
49.nuance: Even the faults, slackness of speech and abuse, are to be kept in measure with one's place; the rule is not to avoid them but to fit them. Family (குடிமை) closes the four measures, so outward conduct is graded by lineage as well as by learning.

items.claim: dress is to fit one's standing, learning, manliness and family
gait is to fit them
slackness of speech is to fit them
rebuke is to fit them

norm.note: a rule of the period that grades outward conduct by one's family rank among other measures

50.reading: The verse says that those of rare learning by listening do not blame others, do not lower themselves, do not sleep among many, do not promise and then hold back, and do not, even by a slip, mock and deride the poor without cause.
50.nuance: இசையாத நேர்ந்து கரவார் is doubtful: it may mean they do not agree to what is unfitting and then hide it, or do not conceal after consenting; தள்ளியும் is read as 'even by a slip'.

51.reading: The verse says that those who want their own radiance do not look at lightning, a falling star, the finery of harlots, or the sun at its rising and setting.
51.nuance: The reason given is the viewer's own lustre (நம்மொளி), not pollution; the harlots' finery sits among dangerous lights in the sky. The sun's முன்னொளி and பின்னொளி are read as its light at dawn and dusk.

items.claim: the flash of lightning is not looked at by those who want their radiance
a falling star is not looked at
the finery of harlots is not looked at
the sun's light at rising is not looked at
the sun's light at setting is not looked at

norm.note: a rule of the period on sights to be avoided, with harlots' adornment among them

52.reading: The verse says that those of unshaken mind never speak deceit, useless words, loose talk, abuse or backbiting.
52.nuance: The five kinds of speech are tied to one cause, a mind that does not waver (அசையாத உள்ளம்); the verse treats bad speech as the sign of an unsteady mind.

items.claim: deceit is never spoken by the steady-minded
useless words are never spoken
loose talk is never spoken
abuse is never spoken
backbiting is never spoken

53.reading: The verse lists acts that those who keep the path do not practise: flicking with the fingers, throwing stones, whistling, calling out, grimacing, anger, concealment, clapping, and harming a limb so that it shows.
53.nuance: Bodily habits and two moral faults, anger and concealment, stand in one list of things not to be made a habit (பயிற்றார்). விகிர்தம் is read as grimacing, and தோன்ற உறுப்புச் செகுத்தல் is uncertain: maltreating a limb in view, or a gesture of the limbs.

items.claim: flicking is not practised by those on the path
stone-throwing is not practised
whistling is not practised
calling out is not practised
grimacing is not practised
anger is not practised
concealment is not practised
clapping the hands is not practised
harming a limb in view is not practised

54.reading: The verse says that a smile, a sweet word, water for the feet, a mat and a bed, these five, are the honours paid together with food to one who has come.
54.nuance: Food is assumed, and the five are what goes with it: the welcome begins with the face and ends with a place to sleep.

items.claim: a smile is an honour paid with food to the guest
a sweet word is such an honour
water for the feet is such an honour
a mat is such an honour
a bed is such an honour

55.reading: The verse says that people of peerless understanding do not wish to stay long at a hostile battlefront, at a drinking bout, in the street of those without a steady mind, where one taken on for his qualities has lost his hold, or at a water's edge where many crowd.
55.nuance: குணநோக்கிக் கொண்டவர் கோள்விட் டுழியும் is unclear; it may be a place where a man chosen for his virtue has been dropped, or where those who chose by virtue have given up their resolve. The rule is about lingering (நீடு நிலை), not entering.

56.reading: The verse says that people do not go into dry grass or forest or kindle fire there, do not run with legs spread when rain falls, do not travel alone through a pathless forest, and, even if the rain fails and poverty swells greatly, do not take up work that departs from their ancestral line.
56.nuance: The verse moves from bodily prudence to a rule of hereditary occupation: தொல்வரவின் தீர்ந்த தொழில், work cut off from the old descent, is barred even in famine. That last line is a birth rule of the period, set beside rules of safety as if of one kind.

norm.note: a rule of the period binding a person to the occupation of his descent even in poverty

57.reading: The verse says that those who wish to be free of disease do not enter alone a ruined house, a temple, the burning ground or the lone old tree that rises by a village road, and do not sleep by day.
57.nuance: The reason given is health, not pollution: the four places are lonely and feared, and தமியர் 'alone' is the condition of the bar.

58.reading: The verse reports that when someone sets out, people do not call after him from behind, do not sneeze, do not even by a slip ask 'where are you going?', do not step in front and speak face to face, and keep their elders on their right on both sides.
58.nuance: The first four rules protect a departure from ill omen; the last, கொள்வர் குரவர் வலம், moves to reverence, keeping the elders on the right. இருசார்வும் may mean going and coming.

norm.note: omen rules of the period for a departure, and the rite of keeping elders on the right

59.reading: The verse reports that people do not say 'my body is well', do not blow out a lamp, do not take fire from a hearth so that it goes out, and do not warm themselves at it with the fire turned toward themselves.
59.nuance: Saying the body is well seems to court misfortune; the last clause, படக்காயார் தம்மேற் குறித்து, is obscure and may bar warming oneself directly at the hearth fire.

norm.note: rules of the period about the household fire and about words that invite ill

60.reading: The verse says that when travelling a road together with the full, self-controlled, elder and eminent, one mounts nothing, wears no sandals and does not shade oneself from the sun.
60.nuance: Deference takes the form of matching the elder's hardship on the road: one gives up mount, sandals and shade beside him.

links.note: Acharakkovai 42 treats the menstrual days as days of no touch and sets the twelve days after the bath apart for the wife; Sivavakkiyar 134 says the monthly pollution is what grows into the body once the months stop, so no birth is free of it.
links.teaches: The ritual rule and the Siddhar's attack both join menstruation to conception, but one draws a line of pollution across the cycle while the other uses the same cycle to deny that any body stands outside pollution.

links.note: Verse 42 names the days a husband keeps to his wife after her bath; verse 43 lists hours and calendar days on which the couple do not come together.
links.teaches: Taken together the two verses make marital union a matter of the ritual calendar, with days prescribed by the wife's cycle and others barred by the moon, the gods and the hours.

links.note: Kural 560 says that when the guardian fails to guard, those of the six duties forget their books; Acharakkovai 47 lists affliction to the land's guardian among the days brahmins do not recite.
links.teaches: Both tie the reciting of the Veda to the king's state: the Kural through long neglect that makes the texts forgotten, the Acharakkovai through a single day of the king's distress that halts recitation at once.
links.list_adds: It sets the king's affliction among moon days, earthquake, thunder and impurity, so the ruler's distress counts as a cosmic disturbance rather than a failure of governance.

links.note: Kural 43 makes tending ancestors, gods, guests, kin and oneself the householder's chief duty; Acharakkovai 48 names the days of gods, ancestors, wedding, festival and sacrifice as days for aram and for feeding guests.
links.teaches: The Kural's standing duties to gods, ancestors and guests are turned by the Acharakkovai into dated occasions, showing how a general householder's duty becomes a festival calendar.
links.list_adds: It replaces the Kural's five persons owed care with five kinds of day, so the duty is counted by occasion, and the guest is fed as an addition to the day's aram.

links.note: Kural 124 praises the restrained man who does not stray from his station (நிலை); Acharakkovai 49 says dress, gait, slack speech and rebuke must fit one's standing (நிலைமை), learning, manliness and family.
links.teaches: The Kural's 'not straying from one's station' is shown in concrete outward marks, and the Acharakkovai's addition of family as a measure shows how that station can be read as rank of birth.
links.list_adds: It names four outward behaviours, two of them faults, and four measures they must fit, so keeping one's station becomes a fitting of dress, walk and speech to learning and lineage.

links.note: Kural 988 says poverty is no disgrace to one with the firmness of worth; Acharakkovai 50 says the learned do not mock or deride the poor.
links.teaches: The disgrace of poverty is denied from two sides: the Kural says the poor man of worth carries none, and the Acharakkovai says the learned onlooker must not lay it on him.
links.list_adds: It sets not deriding the poor among the habits of the learned listener, beside not blaming and not sleeping among crowds, so respect for the poor becomes part of learned decorum.

links.note: Verse 6 bars a falling star from the sight of one in எச்சில்; verse 51 bars a falling star, lightning, harlots' finery and the low sun from anyone who wants to keep his radiance.
links.teaches: The same sight is barred on two grounds in the book, once as a matter of pollution and once to guard one's lustre, so the gaze rules do not rest on pollution alone.

links.note: Kural 196 calls the man who keeps up useless talk chaff among people; Acharakkovai 52 says those of unshaken mind never speak useless words, deceit, loose talk, abuse or backbiting.
links.teaches: The Kural judges the empty talker by what his talk shows him to be, while the Acharakkovai names the cause of not talking so, a steady mind, so useless speech appears as a symptom of an unsettled one.
links.list_adds: It makes useless speech one of five kinds with deceit, wanton talk, abuse and backbiting, all kept off by a single inner steadiness, where the Kural treats useless talk on its own.

links.note: Naladiyar 189 says the pure in heart stay unshaken when slandered; Acharakkovai 52 says those of unshaken mind never backbite.
links.teaches: Held together the two verses make one steady mind both unmoved by slander and unwilling to slander, so steadiness works in both directions of backbiting.
links.list_adds: It sets backbiting last in a list of five faults of speech that the same unshaken mind avoids, where the Naladiyar shows only that mind receiving slander.

links.note: Kural 90 says a guest wilts when the host's face changes; Acharakkovai 54 puts a smile first among five honours given with food to a guest.
links.teaches: The Kural says what the wrong face does to a guest, and the Acharakkovai sets the right face at the head of a sequence of welcome, so the host's smile is the first act of hospitality, before word, water, mat and bed.
links.list_adds: It orders the welcome from face to word to body to rest, so the smile the Kural defends by a negative image becomes the first of five steps that accompany food.

links.note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from the work one does; Acharakkovai 56 says one does not leave the work of one's ancestral line even when famine makes one poor.
links.teaches: If செய்தொழில் in the Kural is occupation, the two clash: the Kural ranks people by their work and not their birth, while the Acharakkovai fixes the work by birth, so rank by work becomes rank by descent.
links.list_adds: It sets the bar on leaving hereditary work after plain rules of safety in fire, rain and forest, treating loyalty to one's descent as prudence of the same kind.

links.note: Verse 16 names the king, teacher, mother, father and elder brother as the குரவர் to be worshipped as gods; verse 58 ends by keeping the குரவர் on one's right.
links.teaches: Verse 16 says the elders are to be worshipped like gods, and verse 58 gives one bodily form of that worship, the circling to the right otherwise paid to the divine.

links.note: Kural 715 calls not speaking first among elders the best restraint; Acharakkovai 60 says that on the road with eminent elders one does not ride, wear sandals or shade oneself.
links.teaches: The Kural's deference to elders lies in speech, the Acharakkovai's in the body on the road, so respect is shown both by holding back the word and by sharing the elder's hardship.
links.list_adds: It turns deference into three bodily refusals, of mount, sandals and shade, which the Kural's single rule about speaking first does not cover.

source_issues: Verse 41 line 2 (தலையோடு றுப்புறுத்த) is damaged; the word division and the sense of the rule are uncertain.
Verse 42 line 3 (பேரறி வாளர் துணிவு) repeats the close of verse 19, a formulaic line.
Verse 44 has doubtful forms (இரியார், பாடஅர்) on lines 1 and 3.
Verse 47 is flagged by the tool as missing from the site edition (site_diff).
Verse 48 names only four occasions plainly against its count of five (ஐவகை).
Verse 55 line 3 and verse 59 line 3 are obscure.
